claim: The G9a/GLP complex mediates mono- and dimethylation of Lys9 of histone H3 at specific gene loci.
source: The G9a/GLP complex mediates mono- and dimethylation of Lys9 of histone H3 at specific gene loci, which is associated with transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Tachibana et al., 2001, 2005; Kubicek et al., 2007) in the introduction.

claim: H3K9 methylation by the G9a/GLP complex is associated with transcriptional repression.
source: The G9a/GLP complex mediates mono- and dimethylation of Lys9 of histone H3 at specific gene loci, which is associated with transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Tachibana et al., 2005, 2008).

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ are two core subunits in the G9a/GLP complex.
source: In this study, with unbiased protein affinity purification, we found ZNF644 and WIZ as two core subunits in the G9a/GLP complex.
evidence: This is supported by affinity purification and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A and 1B, as well as co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 1C.

claim: ZNF644 interacts with the transcription activation domain of G9a.
source: ZNF644 and WIZ interact with the transcription activation domain of G9a and GLP, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by deletion mutant analysis shown in Figure 2B, where the D1 mutant of G9a (lacking TAD) abolishes interaction with ZNF644.

claim: WIZ interacts with the transcription activation domain of GLP.
source: ZNF644 and WIZ interact with the transcription activation domain of G9a and GLP, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by deletion mutant analysis shown in Figure 2E, where only the TAD of GLP is required for interaction with WIZ.

claim: Both ZNF644 and WIZ contain multiple zinc finger motifs that recognize consensus DNA sequences.
source: Moreover, both ZNF644 and WIZ contain multiple zinc finger motifs that recognize consensus DNA sequences.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis identifying consensus DNA-binding motifs (Figure 4H, 4I) and EMSA experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ target G9a and GLP to the chromatin.
source: ZNF644 and WIZ target G9a and GLP to the chromatin and mediate the G9a/GLP complex-dependent H3K9 methylation as well as gene repression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chromatin fractionation experiments in Figure 3B showing that knockdown of ZNF644 and/or WIZ impairs chromatin association of G9a and GLP.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ mediate the G9a/GLP complex-dependent H3K9 methylation.
source: ZNF644 and WIZ target G9a and GLP to the chromatin and mediate the G9a/GLP complex-dependent H3K9 methylation as well as gene repression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP experiments in Figure 5B showing that loss of ZNF644 and WIZ impairs enrichment of H3K9me2 at target loci.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ mediate gene repression by the G9a/GLP complex.
source: ZNF644 and WIZ target G9a and GLP to the chromatin and mediate the G9a/GLP complex-dependent H3K9 methylation as well as gene repression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene expression analysis in Figure 5C showing that loss of ZNF644 and WIZ facilitates gene transcription at target loci.

claim: G9a and GLP are paralogs with similar domain architecture.
source: G9a and GLP are paralogs with similar domain architecture. Both contain a transcription activation domain (TAD), a glutamate-rich domain, a cysteine-rich domain, 7 tandem ankyrin repeats (ANKs), and a methyltransferase domain (Roopra et al., 2004; Dillon et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2006; Purcell et al., 2011; Shinkai and Tachibana, 2011; Bittencourt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural and functional studies.

claim: G9a and GLP form a heterodimer via the interaction between the C-terminal catalytic domains.
source: Interestingly, G9a and GLP form a heterodimer via the interaction between the C-terminal catalytic domains (Tachibana et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The major function of the G9a/GLP complex is to catalyze H3K9me1 and H3K9me2 in euchromatin.
source: The major function of the G9a/GLP complex is to catalyze H3K9me1 and H3K9me2 in euchromatin, which is associated with transcriptional repression (Tachibana et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The G9a/GLP complex regulates multiple biological processes, such as meiosis, embryonic development, immune response, and tumorigenesis.
source: Accumulated evidence has shown that this methyltransferase complex regulates multiple biological processes, such as meiosis, embryonic development, immune response, and tumorigenesis (Tachibana et al., 2002, 2007; Schaefer et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010; Shinkai and Tachibana, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: If one of G9a or GLP is deleted, the other one alone has little enzymatic activity in vivo.
source: Interestingly, if one of these two methyltransferases is deleted, the other one alone has little enzymatic activity in vivo, suggesting that the heterodimer formation is important for the function of this enzyme complex (Tachibana et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Heterodimer formation is important for the function of the G9a/GLP enzyme complex.
source: Interestingly, if one of these two methyltransferases is deleted, the other one alone has little enzymatic activity in vivo, suggesting that the heterodimer formation is important for the function of this enzyme complex (Tachibana et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of one component abolishes activity of the other.

claim: HP1 recognizes H3K9me2.
source: Since HP1 recognizes H3K9me2 (Bannister et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Nielsen et al., 2001), it is likely that the G9a/GLP complex mediates the recruitment of HP1 to specific gene loci for transcriptional repression (Ogawa et al., 2002; Nishio and Walsh, 2004; Shinkai and Tachibana, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The G9a/GLP complex mediates the recruitment of HP1 to specific gene loci for transcriptional repression.
source: Since HP1 recognizes H3K9me2 (Bannister et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Nielsen et al., 2001), it is likely that the G9a/GLP complex mediates the recruitment of HP1 to specific gene loci for transcriptional repression (Ogawa et al., 2002; Nishio and Walsh, 2004; Shinkai and Tachibana, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is demonstrated in the current study by ChIP experiments in Figure 5B.

claim: The ANKs of G9a and GLP recognize H3K9me1 and H3K9me2.
source: Moreover, the ANKs of G9a and GLP also recognize H3K9me1 and H3K9me2 (Collins et al., 2008), which may facilitate the chromatin spreading of the G9a/GLP complex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recognition of H3K9me1 and H3K9me2 by ANKs may facilitate the chromatin spreading of the G9a/GLP complex.
source: Moreover, the ANKs of G9a and GLP also recognize H3K9me1 and H3K9me2 (Collins et al., 2008), which may facilitate the chromatin spreading of the G9a/GLP complex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known function of ANKs.

claim: The G9a/GLP complex is associated with Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2).
source: Recent study suggests that the G9a/GLP complex is associated with Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) (Mozzetta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: EZH2 is the catalytic subunit in the PRC2.
source: EZH2, the catalytic subunit in the PRC2, regulates histone H3K27 methylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: EZH2 regulates histone H3K27 methylation.
source: EZH2, the catalytic subunit in the PRC2, regulates histone H3K27 methylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The G9a/GLP complex and PRC2 methyltransferases function together to modulate histone codes during transcription.
source: Thus, it is likely that these methyltransferases function together to modulate histone codes during transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the association between G9a/GLP and PRC2.

claim: The G9a/GLP complex regulates DNA methylation during early embryogenesis, which is independent of their methyltransferase activity.
source: In addition to histone methylation, the G9a/GLP complex also regulates DNA methylation during early embryogenesis, which is independent of their methyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Esteve et al., 2006; Epsztejn-Litman et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2011).

claim: The G9a/GLP complex associates with DNMT1 through PCNA.
source: It has been reported that the G9a/GLP complex associates with DNMT1 through PCNA (Esteve et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ANKs of G9a interact with DNMT3A and 3B for the de novo DNA methylation.
source: Moreover, the ANKs of G9a interact with DNMT3A and 3B for the de novo DNA methylation (Epsztejn-Litman et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GLP was identified as a partner of G9a in tandem protein affinity purification.
source: Since G9a and GLP form a heterodimer in vivo (Tachibana et al., 2005), we could easily detect GLP as a partner of G9a in this purification, which was served as a positive control.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the purification results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Besides GLP, G9a also interacted with two other proteins identified as ZNF644 and WIZ by mass spectrometry.
source: Interestingly, besides GLP, G9a also interacted with two other proteins. Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that these two proteins were ZNF644 and WIZ, two zinc finger proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the purification and mass spectrometry results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: WIZ has been known to regulate the stability of the G9a/GLP heterodimer.
source: Between these two proteins, WIZ has been known to regulate the stability of the G9a/GLP heterodimer (Ueda et al., 2006), while the function of ZNF644 has not been characterized yet (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The function of ZNF644 has not been characterized prior to this study.
source: Between these two proteins, WIZ has been known to regulate the stability of the G9a/GLP heterodimer (Ueda et al., 2006), while the function of ZNF644 has not been characterized yet (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Reciprocal affinity purification using ZNF644 as bait identified G9a, GLP, and WIZ as binding partners.
source: To validate our initial purification results, we performed reciprocal affinity purification using ZNF644 as the bait. Again, we identified G9a, GLP, and WIZ as binding partners of ZNF644, suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ co-exist in the same complex with G9a and GLP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the purification results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ co-exist in the same complex with G9a and GLP.
source: To validate our initial purification results, we performed reciprocal affinity purification using ZNF644 as the bait. Again, we identified G9a, GLP, and WIZ as binding partners of ZNF644, suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ co-exist in the same complex with G9a and GLP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal purification results and confirmed by co-IP experiments in Figure 1C.

claim: One protein in the G9a/GLP/ZNF644/WIZ complex associates with the other proteins in the complex.
source: We next performed co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays using U2OS cell lysates and found that one protein associated with the other proteins in this complex (Figure 1C), suggesting that these proteins are core subunits in the G9a/GLP complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: G9a, GLP, ZNF644, and WIZ are core subunits in the G9a/GLP complex.
source: We next performed co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays using U2OS cell lysates and found that one protein associated with the other proteins in this complex (Figure 1C), suggesting that these proteins are core subunits in the G9a/GLP complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Down-regulation of G9a or GLP impairs the interaction between WIZ and ZNF644.
source: To further characterize the interactions between these subunits, we knocked down G9a or GLP by siRNAs. Interestingly, down-regulation of G9a or GLP impaired the interaction between WIZ and ZNF644 (Figure 1D), suggesting that the association between WIZ and ZNF644 is mediated by G9a and GLP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments after siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The association between WIZ and ZNF644 is mediated by G9a and GLP.
source: To further characterize the interactions between these subunits, we knocked down G9a or GLP by siRNAs. Interestingly, down-regulation of G9a or GLP impaired the interaction between WIZ and ZNF644 (Figure 1D), suggesting that the association between WIZ and ZNF644 is mediated by G9a and GLP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockdown of G9a or GLP disrupts WIZ-ZNF644 interaction.

claim: The D1 mutant of G9a abolishes the interaction with ZNF644.
source: Interestingly, the D1 mutant of G9a abolished the interaction with ZNF644 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ZNF644 interacts with the TAD of G9a.
source: Since the D1 mutant of G9a lacks the TAD, it suggests that ZNF644 interacts with the TAD of G9a.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion mutant analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lacking the catalytic domain of G9a disrupts the interaction with WIZ.
source: Moreover, lacking the catalytic domain of G9a disrupted the interaction with WIZ (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The catalytic domain of G9a interacts with the catalytic domain of GLP for a heterodimer.
source: However, the catalytic domain of G9a also interacts with the catalytic domain of GLP for a heterodimer.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The association between G9a and WIZ is mediated by GLP.
source: Thus, it is possible that the association between G9a and WIZ is mediated by GLP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the catalytic domain is required for G9a-WIZ interaction and that G9a and GLP form a heterodimer through their catalytic domains.

claim: Lacking G9a, WIZ still interacts with GLP.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we knocked down G9a by siRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Lacking G9a, WIZ still interacted with GLP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that WIZ is likely to directly interact with GLP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments after G9a knockdown shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WIZ is likely to directly interact with GLP.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we knocked down G9a by siRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Lacking G9a, WIZ still interacted with GLP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that WIZ is likely to directly interact with GLP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WIZ-GLP interaction persists in the absence of G9a.

claim: Only the TAD of GLP, but not the catalytic domain of GLP, is required for the interaction with WIZ.
source: Only the TAD of GLP, but not the catalytic domain of GLP, is required for the interaction with WIZ (Figure 2E), suggesting that WIZ recognizes the TAD of GLP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments with GLP deletion mutants shown in Figure 2E.

claim: WIZ recognizes the TAD of GLP.
source: Only the TAD of GLP, but not the catalytic domain of GLP, is required for the interaction with WIZ (Figure 2E), suggesting that WIZ recognizes the TAD of GLP.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion mutant analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The catalytic domain of GLP is required for the interaction with ZNF644.
source: In contrast, the catalytic domain of GLP is required for the interaction with ZNF644 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments with GLP deletion mutants shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ZNF644 directly recognizes the TAD of G9a and associates with GLP via the interactions between G9a and GLP.
source: Since the catalytic domains of G9a and GLP form a heterodimer, it is likely that ZNF644 directly recognizes the TAD of G9a and associates with GLP via the interactions between G9a and GLP.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion mutant analyses and the known heterodimer formation.

claim: The N-terminus of ZNF644 interacts with the TAD of G9a.
source: The D1 mutant of ZNF644 abolished the interaction with G9a (Figure 2G), suggesting that the N-terminus of ZNF644 interacts with the TAD of G9a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IP experiments with ZNF644 deletion mutants shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The C-terminus of WIZ is required for the interaction with GLP.
source: In contrast, the C-terminus of WIZ is required for the interaction with GLP (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IP experiments with WIZ deletion mutants shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Both ZNF644 and WIZ tightly bind to chromatin.
source: Thus, these results indicate that both ZNF644 and WIZ tightly bind to chromatin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3A, where ZNF644 and WIZ remain in the insoluble fraction until Benzonase treatment.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ are chromatin-bound proteins.
source: Interestingly, after treating the insoluble pellets with Benzonase to digest the genomic DNA, both ZNF644 and WIZ were eluted into the soluble fraction, suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ are chromatin-bound proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Approximately 50% of ZNF644 can be eluted from chromatin with 300 mM NaCl treatment.
source: With increased sodium concentration in the lysis buffer, ∼ 50% of ZNF644 was eluted out.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only a small fraction of WIZ can be eluted from chromatin with 300 mM NaCl treatment.
source: However, only a small fraction of WIZ could be eluted from the chromatin, and the remaining WIZ was still tightly associated with genomic DNA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lacking either ZNF644 or WIZ impairs the chromatin association of G9a and GLP.
source: We used siRNAs to knock down ZNF644 and/or WIZ. Lacking either ZNF644 or WIZ impaired the chromatin association of G9a and GLP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments after siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockdown of ZNF644 and WIZ simultaneously remarkably reduces chromatin-bound G9a and GLP.
source: Moreover, when we knocked down ZNF644 and WIZ simultaneously, chromatin-bound G9a and GLP were remarkably reduced, but the levels of soluble G9a and GLP were not affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments after double siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockdown of ZNF644 and WIZ does not affect the levels of soluble G9a and GLP.
source: Moreover, when we knocked down ZNF644 and WIZ simultaneously, chromatin-bound G9a and GLP were remarkably reduced, but the levels of soluble G9a and GLP were not affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Reconstituted cells with siRNA-resistant ZNF644 or WIZ retain G9a in the chromatin fraction.
source: Reconstituted cells with siRNA-resistant ZNF644 or WIZ retained G9a in the chromatin fraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The D1 mutant of ZNF644 is unable to target G9a to chromatin.
source: However, either the D1 mutant of ZNF644 or the D8 mutant of WIZ was able to target G9a to chromatin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments with mutant proteins shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The D8 mutant of WIZ is unable to target G9a to chromatin.
source: However, either the D1 mutant of ZNF644 or the D8 mutant of WIZ was able to target G9a to chromatin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments with mutant proteins shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ facilitate the chromatin localization of the G9a/GLP complex.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that ZNF644 and WIZ facilitate the chromatin localization of the G9a/GLP complex (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the chromatin fractionation and rescue experiments shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: 14,153 G9a enriched regions were identified by ChIP-seq in 293T cells.
source: We identified 14,153 G9a enriched regions, 12,777 ZNF644 enriched regions, and 11,853 WIZ enriched regions, respectively.
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: 12,777 ZNF644 enriched regions were identified by ChIP-seq in 293T cells.
source: We identified 14,153 G9a enriched regions, 12,777 ZNF644 enriched regions, and 11,853 WIZ enriched regions, respectively.
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: 11,853 WIZ enriched regions were identified by ChIP-seq in 293T cells.
source: We identified 14,153 G9a enriched regions, 12,777 ZNF644 enriched regions, and 11,853 WIZ enriched regions, respectively.
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: Approximately 40% of G9a peaks are distributed in gene promoter regions.
source: Approximately, 40% of G9a peaks, 45% of ZNF644 peaks, and 43% of WIZ peaks were distributed in gene promoter region (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Approximately 45% of ZNF644 peaks are distributed in gene promoter regions.
source: Approximately, 40% of G9a peaks, 45% of ZNF644 peaks, and 43% of WIZ peaks were distributed in gene promoter region (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Approximately 43% of WIZ peaks are distributed in gene promoter regions.
source: Approximately, 40% of G9a peaks, 45% of ZNF644 peaks, and 43% of WIZ peaks were distributed in gene promoter region (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Around 54% of WIZ-enriched regions are bound by G9a.
source: We found around 54% of WIZ-enriched regions were bound by G9a, and around 58% of ZNF644 enriched regions were bound by G9a, while around 63% of G9a enriched regions were bound by ZNF644 and/or WIZ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Around 58% of ZNF644 enriched regions are bound by G9a.
source: We found around 54% of WIZ-enriched regions were bound by G9a, and around 58% of ZNF644 enriched regions were bound by G9a, while around 63% of G9a enriched regions were bound by ZNF644 and/or WIZ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Around 63% of G9a enriched regions are bound by ZNF644 and/or WIZ.
source: We found around 54% of WIZ-enriched regions were bound by G9a, and around 58% of ZNF644 enriched regions were bound by G9a, while around 63% of G9a enriched regions were bound by ZNF644 and/or WIZ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most G9a-enriched regions are associated with ZNF644 and/or WIZ.
source: These results indicate that most G9a-enriched regions are associated with ZNF644 and/or WIZ, which is in agreement with our results that the chromatin loading of G9a is dependent on the ZNF644 and/or WIZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: G9a regulates gene transcription via catalyzing H3K9me2 at promoter regions.
source: It has been shown that G9a regulates gene transcription via catalyzing H3K9me2 at promoter regions (Su et al., 2004; Barski et al., 2007; Kubicek et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Around 82% of G9a-enriched peaks in promoter regions are bound by ZNF644 and/or WIZ.
source: Thus, we analyzed G9a peaks in promoter regions and found that around 82% of G9a-enriched peaks in promoter region were bound by ZNF644 and/or WIZ (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is from ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ profiles are associated with G9a profiles in promoter regions.
source: Further analyses across G9a peaks in promoter regions show that ZNF644 and WIZ profiles are also associated with the G9a profiles in promoter region (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profile analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: G9a is clearly associated with ZNF644 and WIZ, especially in promoter regions.
source: Thus, accumulated evidence suggests that G9a is clearly associated with ZNF644 and WIZ, especially in promoter regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq analyses shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: At CWH43, DIP2C and ROCK1 loci, G9a, ZNF644 and WIZ co-localize together at the promoter regions.
source: At CWH43, DIP2C and ROCK1 loci, G9a, ZNF644 and WIZ co-localized together at the promoter regions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq tracks shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At CACNA2D1, ANKRD26P1, USP14, and HCN1 loci, only ZNF644, but little WIZ, significantly co-localizes with G9a in the promoter regions.
source: At CACNA2D1, ANKRD26P1, USP14, and HCN1 loci, only ZNF644, but little WIZ, significantly co-localized with G9a in the promoter regions (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq tracks shown in Figure 4F and ChIP-qPCR in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: At PARD3, ABCA13, SENP5, and NRXN3 loci, WIZ, but little ZNF644, co-localizes with G9a.
source: In contrast, at PARD3, ABCA13, SENP5, and NRXN3 loci, WIZ, but little ZNF644, co-localized with G9a (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq tracks shown in Figure 4G and ChIP-qPCR in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: ZNF644 and/or WIZ associate with G9a at the promoter regions of specific loci.
source: Taken together, ZNF644 and/or WIZ associate with G9 at the promoter regions of specific loci.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR analyses shown in Figures 4E-G.

claim: A specific DNA-binding sequence motif for ZNF644 was identified from ChIP-seq analysis.
source: Using Peak-motifs software (http://floresta.eead.csic.es/rsat/peak-motifs_form.cgi), we examined only ZNF644-enriched regions (lacking WIZ), by which we excluded the possible loading of ZNF644 onto chromatin via WIZ. A specific DNA-binding sequence was concluded by the software (Figure 4H), and this sequence was confirmed at CACNA2D1, ANKRD26P1, USP14, and HCN1 loci only occupied by ZNF644.
evidence: This is from computational analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The ZNF644 DNA-binding sequence was confirmed at CACNA2D1, ANKRD26P1, USP14, and HCN1 loci.
source: A specific DNA-binding sequence was concluded by the software (Figure 4H), and this sequence was confirmed at CACNA2D1, ANKRD26P1, USP14, and HCN1 loci only occupied by ZNF644.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A specific DNA binding sequence of WIZ was obtained from ChIP-seq analysis.
source: Similarly, a specific DNA binding sequence of WIZ was also obtained from software analyses (Figure 4I) and was confirmed at PARD3, ABCA13, SENP5, and NRXN3 loci.
evidence: This is from computational analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The WIZ DNA-binding sequence was confirmed at PARD3, ABCA13, SENP5, and NRXN3 loci.
source: Similarly, a specific DNA binding sequence of WIZ was also obtained from software analyses (Figure 4I) and was confirmed at PARD3, ABCA13, SENP5, and NRXN3 loci.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Both ZNF644 and WIZ-binding sequences were identified at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: Moreover, both ZNF644 and WIZ-binding sequences were identified at the loci co-occupied by ZNF644 and WIZ, such as CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The consensus DNA-binding motifs of ZNF644 and WIZ show strong binding with full-length recombinant proteins.
source: We performed electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA) and found that the consensus DNA-binding motifs of ZNF644 and WIZ showed strong binding with full-length recombinant proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: ZNF644, WIZ, and G9a localize at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: In agreement with the ChIP-seq results, ZNF644, WIZ, and G9a localized at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Down-regulation of ZNF644 and WIZ impairs the localization of G9a at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: Moreover, down-regulation of ZNF644 and WIZ impaired the localization of G9a at these loci (Figure 5A), suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ are important for targeting G9a to this specific loci.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR after siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ are important for targeting G9a to specific loci.
source: Moreover, down-regulation of ZNF644 and WIZ impaired the localization of G9a at these loci (Figure 5A), suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ are important for targeting G9a to this specific loci.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR results after knockdown shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Down-regulation of G9a does not affect the chromatin localization of ZNF644 and WIZ at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: However, down-regulation of G9a did not affect the chromatin localization of ZNF644 and WIZ at these loci (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Both H3K9me2 and HP1α are enriched at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: Since G9a catalyzes H3K9me2 that is recognized by HP1α, we found that both H3K9me2 and HP1α were enriched at these loci.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lacking G9a abolishes the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: Lacking G9a abolished the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR after G9a knockdown shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Loss of ZNF644 and WIZ impairs the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α at CWH43, DIP2C, and ROCK1 loci.
source: Similarly, loss of ZNF644 and WIZ also impaired the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α (Figure 5B), suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ are important for the G9a-dependent H3K9 methylation at G9a targeting genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR after ZNF644/WIZ knockdown shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ are important for the G9a-dependent H3K9 methylation at G9a targeting genes.
source: Similarly, loss of ZNF644 and WIZ also impaired the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α (Figure 5B), suggesting that ZNF644 and WIZ are important for the G9a-dependent H3K9 methylation at G9a targeting genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Down-regulation of G9a increases gene transcription at CWH43, DIP2C and ROCK1 loci.
source: Down-regulation of G9a by siRNA indeed increased gene transcription at these loci (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR after G9a knockdown shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of ZNF644 and WIZ facilitates gene transcription at CWH43, DIP2C and ROCK1 loci.
source: Again, loss of ZNF644 and WIZ also facilitated gene transcription (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR after ZNF644/WIZ knockdown shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ regulate the function of G9a during transcription.

claim: Wild-type ZNF644 and WIZ rescue the recruitment of G9a to CWH43, DIP2C and ROCK1 loci.
source: ZNF644 and WIZ rescued the recruitment of G9a to the gene loci, facilitated the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α, and repressed gene transcription (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The D1 mutant of ZNF644 and the D8 mutant of WIZ fail to restore the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α.
source: However, expression of the D1 mutant of ZNF644 and the D8 mutant of WIZ that abolish the interactions with G9 and GLP, failed to restore the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α as well as transcription repression (Figure 6).

claim: The D1 mutant of ZNF644 and the D8 mutant of WIZ fail to restore transcription repression.
source: However, expression of the D1 mutant of ZNF644 and the D8 mutant of WIZ that abolish the interactions with G9 and GLP, failed to restore the enrichment of H3K9me2 and HP1α as well as transcription repression (Figure 6).

claim: ZNF644 and WIZ are two key subunits in the G9/GLP complex to target G9a and GLP to genomic loci for transcriptional repression.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that ZNF644 and WIZ are two key subunits in the G9/GLP complex to target G9a and GLP to genomic loci for transcriptional repression.

claim: WIZ was previously found to interact with the catalytic domain of G9a.

claim: The interaction between WIZ and G9a is indirect and mediated by the catalytic domain heterodimer of G9a and GLP.
